Nov 24, 2026VCFVMware · AI

VCF 9.1.2 is out#

Broadcom shipped VCF 9.1.2 today. Most of it is about getting AI and Kubernetes platforms running faster, plus two features moving from tech preview to GA.

Quickstarts. Some background: Supervisor is the Kubernetes control plane built into vSphere, and VKS (vSphere Kubernetes Service) uses it to create Kubernetes clusters for application teams. Turning it all on used to mean several separate workflows for networking, load balancing, Supervisor and the first cluster.

  • AI infrastructure quickstart: one vCenter plugin configures the cluster, enables Supervisor and builds a VKS cluster, ready for AI workloads.
  • VKS quickstart: gives you a production-ready Supervisor and VKS cluster, plus a test environment with the common add-ons and a UI to browse it.

Chained VKr upgrades. A VKr (VKS release) is the Kubernetes version a cluster runs. Kubernetes only supports upgrading one minor version at a time, so getting from an old version to a current one means several hops. Now you pick the target version and VCF plans the path, choosing the latest stable patch at each step and keeping add-ons in sync.

GitOps service (GA). Argo CD built into VCF. GitOps means the desired state of your apps and clusters lives in a Git repo, and Argo CD keeps the running environment matching it. Teams can create their own Argo CD instances from VCF Automation, with access through your existing identity provider via OIDC.

vSAN object storage (GA). S3-compatible object storage served from vSAN, with encryption, role-based access and multi-tenancy, provisioned self-service through VCF Automation or YAML.

The object storage is the one I'd pay attention to even if AI isn't on your roadmap. Backup software, log platforms and cloud-native apps increasingly expect an S3 endpoint. Having one inside VCF means you don't need a separate object store on-prem for them.

New on vCloudOne: sizing calculators#

I've added three sizing calculators to the site, one each for Amazon EVS, VMware Cloud on AWS and on-prem VCF.

All three take the same input: RVTools exports, or workload totals typed in by hand. From there they work out how many hosts you need for CPU, memory and storage, add the management overhead the platform runs, apply growth and headroom, and tell you which resource sets the host count.

  • EVS Sizing: hosts and clusters for Amazon EVS, including VCF core counts for licensing.
  • VMC Sizing: SDDCs, clusters and hosts, with workload groups you can place in a specific SDDC or protect to another one for DR, a topology diagram, and a memory tiering estimate per cluster.
  • VCF Sizing: fleets, instances, workload domains and clusters on your own hardware, with licensing and the overhead of add-ons like VCF Operations and NSX Edges.

Everything runs in your browser, so customer data never leaves your machine. Hover over any default to see why it's set that way. The Excel export keeps your settings, so you can load a sizing again later and change it.

I built them for architects and partners who need a first sizing they can defend in a meeting. Confirm with the official tools before anything goes into a quote.

Nov 20, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

You can now raise the Elastic DRS storage warning#

You can now raise the Elastic DRS storage warning on VMware Cloud on AWS from 65% up to 75%.

What Elastic DRS does. Elastic DRS watches each cluster's CPU, memory and storage and adds or removes hosts based on policy. Storage is the one with a hard edge: vSAN needs free space for rebuilds and policy changes. So VMC adds a host automatically when a cluster's storage reaches 80%, whatever your policy says. The warning threshold sends a notification before that point, so you have time to clean up or plan capacity yourself.

The change. The warning used to be fixed at 65%. You can now set it anywhere from 65 to 75 by putting storage_utilization_warning_threshold in the edrs_policy_options_overrides of the cluster's Elastic DRS policy, through the Autoscaler API. KB 463122 has example request bodies.

Why it matters. On storage-heavy clusters, 65% can be normal day-to-day use, so the warning fires constantly and people learn to ignore it. That's the worst outcome for an alert. Setting it closer to where you'd actually act keeps it meaningful. Leave enough room between the warning and the 80% automatic scale-out to respond, especially on clusters that grow fast.

Sources
  • VMware Cloud on AWS release notes: November 20, 2026

Nov 17, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware · AI

Amazon EVS gets r7i hosts, external principal storage and an Agent Skill#

Amazon EVS now supports r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl hosts for VCF 9.x, external principal storage on Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, and an Agent Skill for AI assistants.

r7i hosts. These are memory-optimized hosts on 4th Gen Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids):

  • r7i.metal-24xl: 48 cores, 768 GiB.
  • r7i.metal-48xl: 96 cores, 1,536 GiB.

Unlike i4i and i7i, they have no local NVMe drives at all.

External principal storage. Every VCF cluster needs a principal datastore, the main datastore where its VMs live. Until now on EVS that was always vSAN, built from the NVMe in each host. That meant storage only grew by adding hosts, and you paid for drives whether you needed them or not. With external principal storage, the cluster's main datastore is an FSx for ONTAP volume instead. Hosts without disks, like r7i, become possible, and compute and storage can be sized and scaled separately.

The EVS Deployment Orchestrator can create the FSx file system for you (Single-AZ, in the stack's VPC) or use an existing volume. With FSx, a simple deployment needs only two hosts. ONTAP also brings its own tools, such as snapshots, SnapMirror replication to another Region for DR, and storage efficiency.

Who should look at it. Memory-heavy workloads like databases and in-memory analytics, where vSAN hosts would leave you paying for unused NVMe. Estates that need lots of storage but not much compute. Teams already running FSx for ONTAP.

Agent Skill. AWS also released an Amazon EVS Agent Skill in the Solutions for Amazon EVS repo. Copy it into your AI agent's skills folder and the agent can answer EVS questions from the documentation, citing the page. It can also run EDO deployments in four phases: prepare a validated blueprint and plan, run it after you approve, monitor it and diagnose failures, then handle day-two tasks like adding hosts. It asks before every change and never reads secret values. If you're automating EVS builds, it's worth trying.

vSphere Express, Live Recovery and DR built into VCF#

Broadcom announced three changes to the VCF portfolio in early November.

vSphere Express. A new entry edition built on vSphere 9, for customers with up to 128 cores across all their environments. It includes vMotion, High Availability (VMs restart on another host if one fails), the Distributed Switch, vCenter Quick Patch, and TPM 2.0 and vTPM support. It's aimed at small sites and smaller businesses that need solid virtualization without the full VCF stack.

Two new Advanced Services for VCF:

  • VMware Live Recovery focuses on cyber recovery. When ransomware hits, you can't simply fail over, because the replicas may be infected too. Live Recovery gives you an isolated clean room to bring up recovery points, scan them and find a clean one before restoring to production.
  • VMware Compliance and Configuration Management checks workloads continuously against benchmarks like CIS or your own standards, and fixes drift automatically.

Native disaster recovery. Broadcom plans to build DR orchestration into VCF and VVF themselves, covering recovery of thousands of workloads after outages, hardware failures or human error. It's planned for the next VCF release, with GA estimated for Broadcom's fiscal Q1 2027.

The native DR is the one I'm watching. Today DR on VCF usually means an add-on product with its own licensing. If basic DR orchestration comes built in, recovery designs for both on-prem and EVS get simpler and cheaper.

VMware Cloud on AWS SDDCs will move to version 9.1#

The SDDC software on VMware Cloud on AWS is being upgraded to version 9.1. This is an upgrade of the SDDC software components themselves, not another 1.26 release. Broadcom is still finalizing feature details and will share them in later communications.

The rollout comes in three phases, and the timelines are still being worked out:

  • Early Access: By nomination only, for testing applications in a non-production organization. You ask through your account team or the VMware Cloud on AWS product team, and Broadcom decides who gets in.
  • General Availability: Expected sometime in calendar year 2027. From that point, new SDDCs deploy on 9.1 by default.
  • Fleet Upgrades: Soon after GA, the Fleet Upgrades phase is expected to begin, moving existing SDDCs, including those on 1.26, to 9.1. All new and existing SDDCs, including those on 1.26, are planned to move to 9.1 throughout 2027.

Some rules are already settled. You can't stay on 1.26. This is a managed service, so Broadcom performs the upgrade with advance notice and no action needed on your side. You also can't mix 9.1 and 1.26 clusters in one SDDC, since every cluster in an SDDC has to run the same version. What you can do, once GA is out, is deploy a new 9.1 SDDC next to your existing 1.26 SDDCs until those are upgraded.

The operating model stays the same. Broadcom still handles patching and lifecycle, the uptime SLA stays at 99.9% (99.99% on a stretched cluster), and 24/7 global support and SRE coverage continue. Until your SDDC is upgraded, 1.26 releases keep shipping as usual. Version 9.1 is expected to be supported on i4i, i3en and i7i instances, plus future instance types added to the service.

If you run production on VMC, ask about Early Access now so you can test your applications in a non-production org before fleet upgrades begin. Plan around 2027 but don't treat it as fixed, since the announcement is marked forward-looking and subject to change.

Source
  • Broadcom blog: What's Coming Next: VMware Cloud on AWS SDDC Upgrade to Version 9.1
Nov 2, 2026VCFVMware

VMware Telco Cloud Platform SKUs end, VCF Telco takes over#

Standalone VMware Telco Cloud Platform (TCP) licensing SKUs reached end of availability on November 2, 2026. Telco deployments are now licensed under the standard VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) SKU, using the name VCF Telco.

TCP was a separate, telecom-focused bundle with its own standalone SKU, validated bill of materials, and release cadence, sold in Essentials and Advanced tiers alongside a separate TCP RAN line. While standard enterprise VCF focused on IT workloads, TCP packaged vSphere, vSAN, NSX, VMware Cloud Director, Tanzu Kubernetes Grid (TKGm), and Telco Cloud Automation (TCA) for ETSI-style VNF and CNF orchestration, Kubernetes lifecycle, and carrier data-plane tuning. That tuning covered NSX Enhanced Data Path with DPDK, SR-IOV, Multus secondary networks, real-time kernels, and vCPU pinning, plus PTP and GNSS timing on RAN. Because of that packaging split, many operators ended up running two separate VMware stacks: TCP for network functions and standard VCF for enterprise IT.

TCP is no longer a separate product line. Current and upcoming telco features fold into the standard VCF SKU, putting VNFs, CNFs, IT workloads, and AI on one VCF operating model from data center to edge. Under Broadcom KB 460517, TCP maps to VCF Telco, TCA maps to VCF Telco Services, TKGm maps to VKS, and VMware Cloud Director maps to VCF Automation. On the platform side, VCF Telco includes 2-year LTS on every minor Kubernetes release, NVMe memory tiering without a hardware RAID requirement, compression with global deduplication, and optional vDefend micro-segmentation.

If you already run TCP, nothing changes immediately. Current subscriptions and all of their components stay supported through the transition, and the SKU change shows up at renewal when your environment moves onto the VCF SKU. Ahead of renewal, verify how your existing TCP entitlements and components map to VCF.

Sources

Amazon EVS added four more Regions: Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Taipei), Europe (Spain) and Israel (Tel Aviv).

VCF 9.1.1 lands the week of VMware Explore#

VCF 9.1.1 shipped the same week as VMware Explore in Las Vegas. Most of what's new is aimed at private AI and platform teams.

Multi-tenant model sharing. In VCF Private AI Services, one AI model deployment can now be shared by several tenants or business units. Each gets controlled access to the model without seeing the others' data, and access policy is managed in one place. The point is cost: GPUs are expensive, and running a separate copy of the same model for every team wastes them.

AI Assistant for VCF (tech preview). An assistant inside VCF Operations that helps with diagnostics, for example finding the cause of ESX CPU or memory contention, or making sense of a pile of vMotion errors across vCenter. It can also help build management packs for third-party integrations.

Tech previews: a GitOps service (Argo CD built into VCF, managed from VCF Automation) and native object storage on vSAN. Both went GA in 9.1.2.

For networking teams: EVPN gets a more direct datapath. Transit gateways build VXLAN tunnels straight to the leaf switches, and NAT, load balancing and DHCP relay now work in that mode.

For most infrastructure teams, 9.1.1 is simply the maintenance build to land on after 9.1. The AI features need VCF Private AI Services, so they matter most if private AI is already on your plan.

Aug 27, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

i7i.metal-48xl and the EVS Deployment Orchestrator#

Two launches landed around Amazon EVS's first birthday: a bigger i7i host, and a tool that deploys a full VCF 9 environment from one CloudFormation stack.

i7i.metal-48xl. It's double the 24xl: 96 physical cores on 5th Gen Intel Xeon, 1,536 GiB of memory, twelve 3.75 TB NVMe drives and 100 Gbps of networking. AWS says i7i gives up to 23% better compute and more than 10% better price performance than i4i. A bigger host means fewer hosts for the same work, and with EVS capped at 32 hosts per environment, more capacity fits in one environment. It also leaves more NVMe per host, which helps when you want memory tiering and still need vSAN capacity.

EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO). With VCF 9, EVS provisions the hosts and you install VCF yourself. EDO automates both. You write one YAML blueprint, upload the VCF installer OVA and ovftool to S3, store your Broadcom depot token in Secrets Manager, and launch a CloudFormation stack. A small runner instance then works through nine stages:

  1. AWS networking (5 to 10 minutes): Route 53 zones and records, the Resolver endpoint, DHCP options, NAT and VPC Route Server with BGP peers.
  2. Hosts (45 to 100 minutes): creates the EVS environment and the bare-metal hosts.
  3. VCF (3 to 5.5 hours): deploys the VCF Installer on a temporary datastore, syncs the depot and runs bring-up. That gives you vCenter, vSAN, NSX Manager, SDDC Manager, VCF Operations and an NSX Edge cluster connected to your VPC.

A full build takes about four to seven hours, unattended, and every stage checkpoints, so a failure resumes from where it stopped.

If you need to build EVS environments more than once, for test, DR or several business units, EDO turns a multi-day manual task into an overnight job. Run its quota check first: bare-metal hosts often hit EC2 vCPU quotas.

Aug 21, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Three good reads: NSX Federation, DR and memory tiering on EVS#

In one week in August, AWS published three design posts for Amazon EVS. Together they cover the questions that come up once a migration is done.

NSX Federation (Aug 18). Federation joins several NSX deployments under one Global Manager. You define segments, gateways and distributed firewall rules once, and they apply at every site, whether on-premises or on EVS. Adding a site means registering it with the Global Manager and deploying local Edge nodes, after which existing segments and rules extend to it. For DR, AWS describes Active-Standby Tier-0 gateways with network failover in under a minute, if you automate the NSX and AWS route changes. The firewall rules are already in place at the recovery site when VMs arrive. It's the option for stretching many networks across sites. For a handful of VLANs across two sites, HCX Network Extension is simpler.

DR options (Aug 19). The post lays out four patterns, from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest:

  • Cold: nothing deployed until disaster. Recovery takes 8+ hours, and you lose data back to the last backup.
  • Pilot light: a small EVS environment of 2 to 4 hosts that scales out on failover. About 4+ hours to recover, with minutes of data loss.
  • Warm standby: a smaller cluster sized for critical workloads. About 2+ hours, minutes of data loss.
  • Hot: a full copy of production, recovering in about 15 minutes. Infrastructure-level hot DR needs vSAN stretched clusters, which EVS doesn't have yet.

For tooling, VMware Live Recovery with vSphere Replication gets you about a five-minute RPO, FSx for ONTAP SnapMirror about five minutes, and Veeam CDP a few seconds. A useful tip: run non-critical workloads at the DR site day to day and shut them down in a disaster to free capacity.

Memory tiering (Aug 21). With VCF 9.1, ESX keeps hot memory pages in DRAM and moves cold ones to local NVMe once host memory use passes about 80%. On EVS the default ratio is 1:1, so each host gets as much NVMe memory as it has DRAM, and effective memory doubles. Size against active memory, not consumed memory, and keep active memory under about half of DRAM. Don't combine tiering with memory overcommit.

The EVS-specific catch: vSAN claims all of a host's NVMe at deployment. To use a drive for tiering, you have to evacuate it from vSAN first, and that capacity comes out of your datastore. Plan tiering and storage together, or add an FSx for ONTAP datastore to make up the difference.

Sources
  • AWS blog: Amazon EVS with NSX Federation for Disaster Recovery and Multi-site Networking
  • AWS blog: Disaster Recovery for VMware Workloads on Amazon EVS
  • AWS blog: Increase your cluster density with Memory Tiering in Amazon EVS

Amazon EVS now runs VCF 9.0 and 9.1#

This is the big one for Amazon EVS this year. You can now run VCF 9.0 and 9.1 in every Region where EVS is available.

What changed in the model. With VCF 5.2, EVS deployed the whole stack for you: hosts, networking, vCenter, NSX, vSAN and SDDC Manager. With VCF 9, the work is split. EVS provisions the bare-metal hosts running ESX 9, puts them in your VPC and connects them to the VLANs that form the VCF underlay. You then run Broadcom's VCF Installer and deploy VCF with the same workflow you'd use on-premises. Once the management appliances are up, you create an EVS connector so EVS can see the environment, report license use and enable Windows licensing.

Why it's built this way. Separating infrastructure from software means EVS runs standard VCF 9, deployed the standard way. The skills, runbooks and Broadcom documentation you already use apply as-is, and new VCF releases don't have to wait for EVS to change its deployment automation.

Licensing. You can deploy without license keys and run in evaluation mode, which helps for proofs of concept. Beyond that, you need VCF subscription coverage for the cores you run.

What it unlocks. VCF 9 brings memory tiering, VCF Operations and the rest of the 9.x platform to AWS.

The catch is that the VCF install is now your job. Have the VCF Installer, depot access and your subscription sorted before the hosts are up, because host billing starts when they come online. If you'd rather not do it by hand, the EVS Deployment Orchestrator automates the whole thing.

SDDC 1.26v3: fixes and Secure Boot certificate updates#

SDDC 1.26v3 is a maintenance release for VMware Cloud on AWS, with quality and stability fixes. It's also the first release to deal with an expiring Microsoft Secure Boot certificate.

Secure Boot checks that each piece of boot code is signed by a trusted key before it runs. Many of the keys VMs trust today come from Microsoft certificates issued in 2011, and those certificates expire during 2026. VMs need the newer 2023 certificates in their firmware to keep trusting updated boot components. 1.26v3 starts the platform work for that.

If you run Windows VMs, or Linux VMs that boot through Microsoft's shim, with Secure Boot turned on, read Broadcom KB 423893. It explains the options and what you may need to do inside the guests.

You can now take EVS VCF issues straight to Broadcom#

Until now every Amazon EVS support case went through AWS, whatever the problem was. Now customers with an active VCF subscription can also open VCF software cases directly with Broadcom.

How the two paths split:

  • AWS Support still covers everything: EC2 hosts, VPC networking, the EVS service and API, and the VCF software. It stays the single point of contact if you want one. EVS requires a Business or Enterprise support plan, so you already have it.
  • Broadcom Support covers only the VCF software: vCenter, ESX, NSX, vSAN, SDDC Manager and the rest. You open cases on the Broadcom Support Portal with your VCF subscription entitlements, the same way you would for on-prem VCF.

Why it matters. For a pure VCF software issue, say a vSAN health alarm or an NSX Edge bug, going straight to Broadcom skips a hop and puts you in front of the engineers who own that code. For anything that touches AWS, start with AWS.

Agree on this internally before you need it. Decide which kinds of issues go where, and make sure the people on call have access to the Broadcom portal under the right site.

Amazon EVS environments can now grow to 32 hosts#

The host limit for an Amazon EVS environment went from 16 to 32. You get there by asking for a service quota increase, and it's available in every EVS Region.

An EVS environment is one VCF instance: one management domain with vCenter, NSX, SDDC Manager and VCF Operations, and the hosts and clusters it manages. The 32 hosts can be one large cluster or several smaller ones across VCF domains.

Why it matters. Every environment carries its own management stack. That's management VMs eating capacity, appliances to patch and upgrade, and another set of DNS records, BGP peers and certificates to look after. If you needed more than 16 hosts, you had to run two environments and pay that overhead twice. Now many estates fit in one.

Watch the quota. It's a quota, so it isn't automatic, and it isn't the only one that applies. Bare-metal hosts count against your EC2 On-Demand vCPU quota too, so check both before a large build. If you need more than 32 hosts in one VCF domain, you still need to design around the limit.

May 5, 2026VCFVMware · AI

VCF 9.1 is here#

Broadcom announced VCF 9.1 on May 5, the first feature release after 9.0. These are the parts I'd look at first.

Memory tiering grows up. Memory tiering lets ESX use local NVMe as a second, slower tier of memory. A tiering engine watches which memory pages VMs actually use. Busy ("hot") pages stay in DRAM, and idle ("cold") pages move to NVMe. Most VMs touch only a fraction of their memory at any moment, so a host can run more VMs than its DRAM alone would allow. In 9.1 you can mirror the tier device in software across two NVMe drives, so losing one drive doesn't take memory with it, and there's built-in analysis of the cost savings. It's the feature that makes cluster density on cloud hosts look very different.

vSAN data reduction on more clusters. Inline deduplication and compression now work on more cluster types and workload profiles, and deduplication now works with data-at-rest encryption. Less raw capacity per usable terabyte means fewer hosts for storage-bound clusters.

Live patching. On hosts with a TPM, many ESX patches can be applied to the running kernel without evacuating the host. Broadcom says this covers up to 80% of patches. For large clusters that's a big cut in maintenance time.

Ransomware recovery on-prem. Cyber recovery now works with isolated clean rooms inside VCF, so you can test and recover workloads in a quarantined environment before putting them back.

Also new: faster VM and Kubernetes deployment using linked clones, larger fleet and upgrade scale, and native S3-compatible object storage on vSAN as a tech preview.

9.1 is also one of the two VCF 9 versions Amazon EVS added in July, so if you're planning EVS on VCF 9, start here. The 9.1.x line has continued since, with 9.1.1 in September and 9.1.2 in November.

Amazon EVS adds the i7i.metal-24xl#

Amazon EVS now supports i7i.metal-24xl, a smaller host than the i4i.metal it launched with, on a newer CPU.

How they compare:

  • i4i.metal: 3rd Gen Intel Xeon (Ice Lake), 64 physical cores, 1,024 GiB of memory and eight 3.75 TB NVMe drives.
  • i7i.metal-24xl: 5th Gen Xeon (Emerald Rapids), 48 physical cores, 768 GiB and six 3.75 TB drives.

AWS says i7i delivers up to 23% better compute performance and more than 10% better price performance than i4i.

Why a smaller host helps. VCF is subscribed per physical core, so on EVS your bill has two parts: the EC2 hosts and the VCF cores on them. A host with fewer but faster cores can do the same work while licensing fewer cores. That matters most for CPU-bound workloads, where the newer chip does more per core. Memory per core is the same on both, 16 GiB, so a memory-bound estate simply needs more i7i hosts than i4i hosts for the same total memory, and the licensing saving is smaller.

Run your own sizing both ways. For many estates, the i7i option comes out ahead on total cost once VCF cores are counted.

Apr 20, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Windows Server licenses on Amazon EVS#

You can now license Windows Server through AWS for VMs running on Amazon EVS, and pay per vCPU-hour while each VM runs.

Why it's needed. Running Windows Server on dedicated hosts in the cloud depends on license portability. Licenses with portability rights can be brought to EVS (BYOL), and AWS doesn't charge extra for those VMs. Many customers have VMs whose licenses can't move. Until now, those needed a separate licensing arrangement before they could migrate.

How it works.

  • Connector: you create an EVS connector to vCenter. It's a read-only link: a vCenter SSO user in the ReadOnly group, with its credentials in Secrets Manager. EVS uses it to watch VM power state and vCPU count.
  • Entitlements: you create entitlements listing which VMs are licensed through AWS, up to 100 VMs each.
  • Billing: by vCPU-hour, only while the VM is powered on.
  • Activation: the VMs activate against an AWS KMS host. You create a VPC interface endpoint for the EVS Windows activation service, allow TCP 1688 from the VMs, then point each VM at it with slmgr /skms and slmgr /ato. Group Policy or a script handles that at scale.

Why it matters. Licensing is often what blocks a Windows-heavy migration, and this removes that blocker without a new agreement. Because billing follows power state and vCPU count, right-sizing VMs and switching off idle ones now saves licence cost directly.

If you have Windows VMs without portability rights, this is probably the simplest way to cover them on EVS. Run BYOL VMs alongside them if you have eligible licenses, since those carry no extra AWS charge.

Apr 16, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

Usage Report APIs for VMware Cloud on AWS#

VMware Cloud on AWS now has three usage report APIs, so you can pull consumption data into your own tools instead of waiting for the invoice.

They all follow the same pattern, GET /activityanalytic/{org_id}/<type>/{freq}/usage-report, return daily data, and accept up to 31 days per call:

  • Host usage (/hosts/): the daily maximum number of hosts per instance type and Region group across all your SDDCs, with your subscription count next to it and any overage. Data goes back to February 2025.
  • Microsoft SPLA usage (/spla/): daily Windows Server Datacenter and SQL Server Enterprise license usage per instance type and SDDC. SKUs look like VOD-I4I-MSFT-SQL. Data from January 2026.
  • Miscellaneous usage (/misc/): the charges that aren't hosts, like internet egress, cross-Region transfer, Direct Connect data, Elastic IPs and Transit Connect. Data from January 2026.

The host report is the useful one for most people. Comparing actual hosts against subscribed hosts every day shows overage as it happens, which is when you can still do something about it. The misc report is where surprises usually come from, especially egress and Transit Connect.

If you run FinOps dashboards, wire these into the same place as the rest of your cloud spend. If you just want a readable report, Broadcom has a command-line tool that turns all three into an HTML report (KB 437094).

Sources

HCX 4.11.4 for VMware Cloud on AWS#

HCX 4.11.4 is a maintenance release for VMware Cloud on AWS. Like 4.11.3, it ships without the WAN optimization appliance.

WAN-OPT used to sit in an HCX service mesh and compress and dedupe migration traffic, which mattered on slow or expensive links. On a fast Direct Connect link it added little, and Broadcom has now retired it.

If a service mesh still includes WAN-OPT, remove it from the mesh and its compute profile before you upgrade. If you're mid-migration over a thin link, expect transfers to take longer without it, and plan migration waves around that.

Apr 1, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

i7i.metal-24xl comes to VMware Cloud on AWS#

With SDDC 1.26v2, VMware Cloud on AWS supports a new host type, i7i.metal-24xl, for new SDDCs and existing ones.

What the host is. It runs on 5th Gen Intel Xeon (Emerald Rapids), with 48 physical cores and hyper-threading on by default, so vSphere sees 96 logical CPUs. It has 768 GiB of DDR5 memory, six 3.75 TB NVMe drives and 56.25 Gbps of networking. Broadcom estimates a three-host cluster gives about 13 TB usable on vSAN OSA and about 20 TB on vSAN ESA. The exact number depends on your storage policy and how well your data compresses.

Where it fits. Compared with i4i.metal, it's a smaller host with fewer cores on a newer, faster CPU. That suits workloads licensed per core, like SQL Server and Oracle. On secondary clusters you can also cap the cores used per host: 8, 16, 24, 30 or 36 on clusters of three or more hosts, and 16, 24, 30 or 36 on two-host clusters. Fewer licensed cores can save more than the host costs.

Getting there. Existing SDDCs must be on 1.26v2 first. A new SDDC defaults to vSAN ESA and can start at two hosts. Stretched clusters on i7i are opt-in and use vSAN OSA. To move from i3, i3en or i4i, add an i7i cluster and vMotion the VMs across, or ask for the cluster conversion service where it's eligible. Clusters already on VM hardware version 21 can't be converted from i4i to i7i.

If you're on i3 or i3en, this is the host to look at for your refresh. Check the Region list too: it's available in most major Regions, but not all of them.

Amazon EVS deployment prerequisites guide#

I wrote up everything Amazon EVS checks before it will deploy VCF 5.x, in the order you'll need it.

EVS validates a lot before it builds anything: the account and support plan, IAM permissions, the VPC and its subnets, the service access subnet, Route 53 zones and records for every host and appliance, the inbound Resolver endpoint, DHCP options, the VPC Route Server and its BGP peers, the capacity reservation for the bare-metal hosts, the VCF license, and the EC2 key pair. If any of those is wrong, the deployment fails and you start again. Most first attempts fail on DNS or on Route Server.

The guide walks through each prerequisite with screenshots and explains why EVS needs it. It comes with a Terraform kit that builds the AWS side as code, and a validator that checks an account before you call CreateEnvironment.

One note on versions. This guide is for the VCF 5.x flow, where EVS runs the whole deployment. For VCF 9, EVS only provisions the hosts and networking, and you install VCF yourself with the VCF Installer or the EVS Deployment Orchestrator. Most of the AWS-side prerequisites still apply, though.

Jan 23, 2026Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Multiple NSX Tier-0 gateways on Amazon EVS#

Amazon EVS now supports more than one NSX Tier-0 gateway in an environment, each on its own NSX Edge cluster.

Some background first. In NSX, VMs connect to overlay segments, and segments attach to Tier-1 gateways, which handle routing between those segments. The Tier-0 gateway sits above them and is the way in and out: it routes traffic between the overlay and everything outside it. On EVS, that means the Tier-0 exchanges routes with your VPC over BGP, through VPC Route Server. A Tier-0 runs on Edge nodes, the VMs that do the actual packet forwarding and services like NAT.

Until now, all of an environment's north-south traffic went through one Tier-0 and one Edge cluster. That's a single throughput ceiling, and a single routing and security domain shared by everything.

With multiple Tier-0s you can split that up. Traffic can be spread across Edge clusters for more total throughput. Production and non-production can sit behind different gateways with different routing and firewall policies. And you can stand up a separate gateway to test a configuration change or a gateway upgrade without touching the one production uses.

The cost is more Edge nodes to run and more BGP sessions to manage, so it's worth it when you need the isolation or the throughput, not by default. AWS has a re:Post article on deploying a second Edge cluster in EVS.

Sources

Jan 20, 2026VCFVMware

VCF 9.0.2 maintenance release#

VCF 9.0.2 is mostly a fix release, but two changes in vCenter 9.0.2 remove common causes of trouble.

Certificates renew themselves. vCenter and ESX use TLS certificates that the built-in VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) issues. When they expire, things break: hosts disconnect, logins fail, and it usually happens at an awkward time. From 9.0.2, vCenter's machine SSL certificate is extended by two years once it's within five days of expiring. ESX host certificates are extended by five years once they're within ten days, on hosts that support renewal without disruption. This only works in VMCA certificate mode. If you switched to custom certificates, it won't happen, and you'll need to set the mode back to "vmca" to get it.

Supervisor backup is on by default. Supervisor is the Kubernetes control plane built into vSphere. Its data is now backed up alongside the vCenter file-based backup by default, so restoring vCenter doesn't leave Supervisor broken.

The release also fixes several login problems, including one caused by the 90-day OAuth credential rotation in VCF SSO, and vpxd crashes when automation makes parallel API calls. If you're on 9.0.0 or 9.0.1, plan for 9.0.2. If you use custom certificates, the auto-renewal won't help you, so keep tracking expiry dates.

Source

Pick your VCF and ESX versions on Amazon EVS#

Amazon EVS now lets you pick a supported combination of VCF and ESX versions instead of always getting whatever EVS deploys by default. This launch also added VCF 5.2.2 for new environments.

It works through three APIs. GetVersions lists the combinations EVS supports. CreateEnvironment takes the VCF version when you build a new environment. CreateEnvironmentHost takes the ESX version when you add hosts to an existing one.

Why it matters: a migration goes more smoothly when the target runs the same version as the source. HCX, vMotion compatibility and your runbooks all behave more predictably when on-prem and EVS match. It also matters on day two. When you add hosts months after the first build, you want them on the same ESX build as the rest of the cluster, not a newer one that leaves the cluster running mixed builds until you upgrade it.

If you automate EVS builds, call GetVersions first and pin the version in your templates rather than relying on the default.

Source

Jan 16, 2026VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

SDDC 1.26: vSAN ESA, bring your own key and VM hardware 21#

SDDC 1.26 moves VMware Cloud on AWS to vSphere 8.0 Update 3. It's the biggest platform release VMC has had in a while, and it changes how you size storage.

vSAN ESA. vSAN has two architectures. The Original Storage Architecture (OSA) splits each host's drives into a cache tier and a capacity tier, organized in disk groups. The Express Storage Architecture (ESA) was built for fast NVMe: there's no cache tier, every drive adds capacity, and compression and snapshots are built into how data is stored. In 1.26, ESA is the default for new i4i.metal SDDCs, but only for SDDCs in a single AZ. Stretched clusters stay on OSA.

The practical difference is RAID-5. On ESA, RAID-5 works from three hosts using a 2+1 layout: two data blocks and one parity block. You can lose a host and keep running, and only a third of the raw space goes to protection. On OSA, three hosts usually means RAID-1 mirroring, which uses half. So a small ESA cluster gets noticeably more usable storage from the same hosts. ESA also always verifies checksums, and the per-host component limit goes from 9,000 to 27,000.

Bring your own key. You can now encrypt VMs with keys from your own KMIP-compliant key management system, through vSphere VM Encryption. That covers workload VMs. The VMC control plane still uses AWS KMS for vSAN encryption, managed by Broadcom. If you migrate encrypted VMs with HCX bulk migration, both SDDCs need the same key provider.

VM hardware version 21. VMs can have up to 256 disks (64 per NVMe controller across four controllers), up from 60, and NVMe disks can now be used for Windows Server Failover Clustering. The upgrade is one-way and needs the VM powered off, so only do it for VMs that need these limits, and test first.

VMware Tools 12.5.4 ships with it.

If you're starting a new single-AZ SDDC, ESA is the default and worth it. If you have a security team that wants to hold its own encryption keys, BYOK is the feature they've been asking for.

Sources
  • Broadcom blog: VMware Cloud on AWS: SDDC Version 1.26 Release
  • VMware Cloud on AWS release notes: January 16, 2026

Dec 15, 2025Amazon EVSHyperscalers · VMware

Amazon EVS adds seven Regions#

Amazon EVS is now in seven more Regions: US West (N. California), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan), Mexico (Central) and South America (São Paulo).

A quick reminder of how EVS uses a Region. An EVS environment runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts in your own VPC, inside one Availability Zone, so the Region decides where your VMs and their data physically live. It also decides what's close by: the AWS services your VMs will talk to, and the Direct Connect locations you'll use to reach on-premises.

That makes Region coverage a real factor for three kinds of projects: data residency, where data has to stay in a country; latency, where apps need to sit near users or other systems; and disaster recovery, where you want a second environment in a nearby Region. Before you plan on one of these Regions, check that the host type you want is offered there. Not every Region carries every EC2 metal instance.

Dec 2, 2025VMware Cloud on AWSHyperscalers · VMware

VMware Cloud on AWS: December 2025 roundup#

Broadcom's December roundup for VMware Cloud on AWS had four changes worth knowing about. Two of them affect how you design and pay for an SDDC.

Smaller stretched clusters. A stretched cluster spreads one vSAN cluster across two Availability Zones, with a witness in a third AZ that breaks ties if the two sides lose contact. Every write goes to both AZs, so if one AZ fails, the VMs restart in the other with no data loss. The catch has always been the entry cost: the floor was six hosts. Now a stretched cluster can scale down to four hosts (two per AZ) or even two (one per AZ), as long as resources allow it. There are exceptions. Clusters running Large management appliances still need six hosts, and clusters with custom CPU core counts set to eight need four. You also can't scale down a cluster that's already close to its resource thresholds.

HCX 4.11.3 drops WAN optimization. HCX is the migration tool most people use to move VMs into VMC. The WAN-OPT appliance used to sit in the service mesh and compress and dedupe migration traffic over slower links. It's gone in 4.11.3, which is now the only upgrade target and is supported until October 11, 2027. Before you upgrade, remove WAN-OPT from every service mesh and compute profile, or the upgrade won't go cleanly.

Better i3 conversion estimates. i3.metal is the oldest host type on VMC. The updated VMC Sizer now looks at six resource dimensions, and whichever one is tightest sets the host count. Moving to i4i.metal or i3en.metal often needs fewer hosts, because the newer hosts have more cores, memory and storage each. Treat the numbers as a planning estimate. Final counts are checked during the conversion itself.

The fourth change is cosmetic but welcome: a redesigned console at vmc.broadcom.com.

If you've held off on stretched clusters because of the six-host minimum, run the numbers again. And if you're still on i3, the conversion estimate is a quick way to see what moving off it would cost.

Source
